subject: chemistry
title: States of matter and changes of state
key_idea: Matter is a solid, a liquid or a gas, depending on how its particles are arranged, how they move and how strongly they attract each other. Changing state is a physical change. The stronger the forces between particles, the higher the melting point and boiling point.

blocks.text: The particle model shows each state as small solid spheres. This section covers how the spheres are arranged and how they move in each state.

items.meaning: An atom, molecule or ion, drawn as a small solid sphere in the model.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. Freezing happens at the same temperature.
The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas. Condensing happens at the same temperature.

rows: Move around and past each other
Flows, takes the shape of its container, cannot be compressed

items: In a solid the particles are in fixed positions and only vibrate.
In a liquid the particles are close but can move past each other.
In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly, so a gas fills any container.

blocks.text: Each change of state has a name. This section covers the names, what happens to the particles, and why the changes are physical.

items: Heating gives the particles more energy, so they move faster.
At the melting or boiling point the particles have enough energy to overcome the forces between them.
The stronger the forces, the more energy is needed, so the higher the melting point and boiling point.
A giant structure has strong bonds throughout, so its melting point is high. A simple molecule has weak forces between its molecules, so its melting and boiling points are low.
Cooling does the reverse: the particles lose energy and the forces pull them together.
A change of state is a **physical change**. No new substance is made and the change can be reversed.
The particles stay the same. They only gain or lose energy.
A **chemical change** makes a new substance and is not easily reversed.

diagram.alt: Move the temperature slider to heat or cool ethanol and watch its particles change between solid, liquid and gas.

items: Melting and boiling need energy to overcome the forces between particles.
Stronger forces mean a higher melting point and boiling point.
Changes of state are physical: the same substance, easily reversed.

sections.heading: Using data and the limits of the model

blocks.text: Melting and boiling points tell you the state of a substance at any temperature. This section covers how to read them, and where the particle model falls short.

items.text: Compare the temperature with the melting point and the boiling point.

blocks.text: Ethanol melts at -114 °C and boils at 78 °C. At 25 °C it is above one and below the other, so it is a liquid.
Limitations of the particle model (Higher tier for AQA)

items: It does not show the forces of attraction between particles.
It shows every particle as a solid, inelastic sphere, but particles are not all spheres and not all the same size.
It does not show the size of the particles compared with the space between them.

blocks.text: Melting point and boiling point are bulk properties. A single atom or molecule does not have a boiling point.

items: Compare the temperature with the melting and boiling points to name the state.
The model leaves out forces and treats all particles as identical solid spheres.
A boiling point belongs to a large number of particles, not to one.

checks.q: Describe how the particles move and are arranged in a liquid.
checks.a: The particles are close together in a random arrangement. They move around and past each other.

checks.q: Explain why melting is a physical change and not a chemical change.
checks.a: No new substance is made, and the change can be reversed.

checks.q: Oxygen melts at -219 °C and boils at -183 °C. State its state at -200 °C and explain how you know.
checks.a: It is a liquid, because -200 °C is above the melting point and below the boiling point.

worked_example.question: Explain why water vapour and not liquid water is produced when diesel burns.
answer_points: Diesel burns at a high temperature, greater than 100 °C.
This is above the boiling point of water, so the water is a gas.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the high temperature and one for comparing it with the boiling point of water.

worked_example.question: Crystals of copper sulfate are made when some water is removed from an aqueous solution of copper sulfate. Describe how the arrangement and movement of the particles change as crystals are formed from a solution.
answer_points: In the solution the ions are moving freely.
In the solution the ions are randomly arranged.
In the solid the ions are fixed or vibrating.
In the solid the ions are in a regular arrangement, a lattice.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. Say ions, atoms or particles, not molecules.

worked_example.question: Carbon dioxide changes state from a solid to a gas at -78 °C. Changing state from a solid to a gas is called subliming. Describe what happens to the movement and arrangement of the particles when a solid turns into a gas. Use the particle model.
answer_points: The particles move faster in the gas and more slowly in the solid.
The particles have more energy in the gas.
The particles are further apart in the gas and closer together in the solid.
The particles are arranged more randomly in the gas and regularly in the solid.
The forces between the particles are weaker in the gas.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. Answers must compare the gas with the solid.
